summary: Genesis presents a rich field for theologically motivated textual revision across all major traditions, with the LXX, Targums, Peshitta, and Vulgate each exhibiting characteristic strategies. The dominant interventions cluster around anthropomorphism avoidance (especially in the Targums and LXX), messianic heightening at key oracular texts (Gen 3:15; 49:10), and harmonization of narrative tensions in the Samaritan Pentateuch. Tradents across traditions were particularly sensitive to passages depicting God in corporeal or emotionally reactive terms, and to proto-messianic ambiguities in the patriarchal blessings.
summary_plain: Scribes and translators working with Genesis made deliberate changes to the text for theological reasons. They softened descriptions of God having a human body or emotions, added messianic overtones to certain prophecies, and smoothed out tensions between stories. These changes can be traced across the ancient Jewish, Christian, and Samaritan versions of the text.

revisions.mt_reading: הוּא יְשׁוּפְךָ רֹאשׁ — 'he (the seed/offspring) will strike your head'
revisions.revised_reading: ipsa conteret caput tuum — 'she (the woman) will crush your head'
revisions.evidence: Jerome's use of 'ipsa' (feminine singular) instead of the expected 'ipse' (masculine, matching 'semen'/'seed') introduces a Marian-messianic reading unprecedented in the Hebrew or Greek traditions. The LXX uses 'autos' (masculine), consistent with a reference to the seed/descendant. Jerome's feminine pronoun redirects the crushing agent from the Messiah (or his seed) to the Virgin Mary, a reading that became foundational in Catholic Mariology. Some Vulgate manuscripts do read 'ipse,' and textual critics have debated whether 'ipsa' reflects Jerome's original or a later scribal insertion, but the Marian trajectory is clearly theologically motivated. The shift cannot be explained by normal translation conventions from the Hebrew.
revisions.evidence_plain: Jerome's Latin Bible changed 'he' (referring to the offspring) to 'she' (the woman/Mary), turning this verse into a prophecy about the Virgin Mary crushing the serpent's head. This is not supported by the Hebrew or Greek texts and reflects early Christian Marian theology.
scholarly_citations: Westermann, Genesis 1–11, pp. 259–260
Hengel & Schwemer, Jesus und das Judentum, pp. 44–45
Speiser, Genesis (AB), p. 25
de Waard & Nida, A Translator's Handbook on Genesis, p. 67
revisions.counter_arguments: Some manuscripts read 'ipse' rather than 'ipsa,' and Jerome himself in his commentaries seems aware of the masculine reading; 'ipsa' may be a post-Hieronymian scribal correction influenced by Marian piety rather than Jerome's own theological revision.

revisions.mt_reading: עַד כִּי-יָבֹא שִׁילֹה — 'until Shiloh comes' or 'until he comes to Shiloh' (highly disputed)
revisions.revised_reading: ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ τὰ ἀποκείμενα αὐτῷ — 'until the things reserved/stored up for him come' (or in some LXX witnesses: 'until he comes for whom it is reserved')
revisions.evidence: The MT's 'Shiloh' (שִׁילֹה) is rendered by the LXX as 'ta apokeimena auto' ('the things stored up for him'), a phrase echoing Ezekiel 21:32 (LXX 21:27: 'ἕως οὗ ἔλθῃ ᾧ τὰ ἀπόκειται') and orienting the passage toward an eschatological ruler figure. This is not a straightforward translation of any plausible Hebrew Vorlage but represents an interpretive move that transforms a geographic or personal name into a title of eschatological expectation. The Targums (Onkelos, Ps-Jonathan, Neofiti) similarly render this as a messianic figure: 'until the Messiah comes, to whom the kingdom belongs.' The convergence across traditions on a messianic reading, where the Hebrew is ambiguous or obscure, strongly indicates theologically motivated revision. Schaper and van der Kooij have both noted that eschatological-messianic sharpening of such oracles is characteristic of Hellenistic-era translators.
revisions.evidence_plain: The Hebrew is ambiguous—possibly a place name or a personal name—but translators in Greek and Aramaic consistently turned it into a prophecy about a coming Messiah or royal figure. This shows deliberate theological updating of an obscure text.
scholarly_citations: Schaper, Eschatology in the Greek Psalter, pp. 18–22 (on LXX messianic hermeneutics)
van der Kooij, The Oracle of Tyre, pp. 30–35
Hamilton, The Book of Genesis 18–50 (NICOT), pp. 653–658
Fitzmyer, The Genesis Apocryphon, p. 112
revisions.counter_arguments: The MT itself is textually uncertain, and 'Shiloh' may already be a title meaning 'the one to whom it belongs' (reading שֶׁלּוֹ), in which case the LXX and Targums may be translating a variant Hebrew text rather than making a theologically motivated change.

revisions.mt_reading: וַיִּנָּחֶם יְהוָה כִּי-עָשָׂה אֶת-הָאָדָם — 'And YHWH repented/was grieved that he had made humankind'
revisions.revised_reading: Onkelos: וְאִתְנַחַם קֳדָם יְיָ — 'And it was regretted before the LORD'; Ps-Jonathan: replaces naham with a distancing formula, avoiding any statement of divine emotional change
revisions.evidence: The root נחם in this context implies divine regret or change of mind—a patently anthropopathic formulation. Targum Onkelos consistently employs the 'before the LORD' (קֳדָם יְיָ) distancing formula to remove the emotional subject from God and instead posit an impersonal expression of divine displeasure. This is a well-documented Targumic strategy for avoiding anthropopathism, catalogued extensively by Kuiper, Klein, and Hayward. The LXX renders it ἐνεθυμήθη ('he reflected/considered'), which is less emotionally charged than the MT's naham, also showing sensitivity. The motivation is clearly theological: the translators found it problematic to ascribe regret or change of mind to the immutable God.
revisions.evidence_plain: The Hebrew says God 'regretted' making humans, which troubled ancient Jewish translators who believed God cannot change his mind. The Aramaic paraphrase carefully avoids saying God felt regret directly, instead saying something more like 'there was regret before God.'
scholarly_citations: Kuiper, The Pseudo-Jonathan Targum and Its Relationship to Onkelos, pp. 45–52
Klein, The Fragment-Targums of the Pentateuch, vol. 1, pp. 33–34
Hayward, Divine Name and Presence: The Memra, pp. 60–65
Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, pp. 174–176
revisions.counter_arguments: The Targumic 'before the LORD' formula occurs so frequently as a standard rendering convention that some scholars argue it is a fixed translation idiom rather than evidence of theological anxiety in any given passage.

revisions.mt_reading: וַיֵּרָא אֵלָיו יְהוָה ... וַיִּשָּׂא עֵינָיו וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה שְׁלֹשָׁה אֲנָשִׁים — 'And YHWH appeared to him ... he lifted his eyes and saw three men.' The narrative oscillates between YHWH's direct presence and the three men, implying corporeal divine visitation; Abraham serves food directly to the visitors.
revisions.revised_reading: Targum Ps-Jonathan and Neofiti introduce the Memra ('Word') of the LORD as the mediating agent, so that it is the Memra that appears, not YHWH directly. The divine anthropomorphic presence is consistently filtered through this theological abstraction.
revisions.evidence: The MT's theophanic narrative presents YHWH eating food (v. 8) and conversing with Abraham in an apparently physical form—among the most theologically challenging anthropomorphisms in the Pentateuch. Targumic tradition systematically introduces the Memra as a buffer between the transcendent deity and narrative physicality. Hayward's monograph on the Memra demonstrates that this is a deliberate theological construct, not a Hebrew Vorlage variant. The LXX preserves the anthropomorphism more directly but softens the scene by clarifying the distinction between YHWH and the angels. The Targums' deployment of Memra at precisely these high-tension anthropomorphic nodes is the clearest evidence of theological motivation.
revisions.evidence_plain: This passage describes God appearing in human form and eating a meal with Abraham, which was deeply uncomfortable for later Jewish theology. Aramaic translators inserted the concept of God's 'Word' (Memra) as a kind of stand-in so that God himself was not depicted in physical human terms.
scholarly_citations: Hayward, Divine Name and Presence: The Memra, pp. 28–52
McNamara, Targum Neofiti 1: Genesis, pp. 103–106
Segal, Two Powers in Heaven, pp. 35–38
Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, pp. 172–180
revisions.counter_arguments: Some scholars, following Boyarin, argue the Memra is not primarily an anti-anthropomorphic device but a full theological hypostasis with its own positive theological content, meaning its deployment here may not be primarily defensive.

revisions.mt_reading: וַיְכַל אֱלֹהִים בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי מְלַאכְתּוֹ — 'And God finished on the seventh day his work'
revisions.revised_reading: LXX: καὶ συνετέλεσεν ὁ θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἕκτῃ — 'And God finished on the sixth day'
revisions.evidence: The LXX reads 'sixth day' instead of 'seventh day,' a change also attested in SP and Peshitta. The MT implies that some work was done on the seventh day before its completion, which contradicts the sanctity of the Sabbath as a day of complete rest. The LXX's harmonizing change ensures that all work was complete before the seventh day began, protecting Sabbath theology. This is a clear case where the theological problem (work occurring on the Sabbath) drives the textual change. Wevers' critical commentary on LXX Genesis explicitly identifies this as harmonization. De Waard notes the cross-tradition attestation strengthens the case for independent theological convergence rather than shared Vorlage.
revisions.evidence_plain: The Hebrew says God finished his work 'on the seventh day,' but the Greek, Samaritan, and Syriac versions all say 'sixth day.' This change was made to avoid the implication that God worked on the Sabbath, which would contradict the law of Sabbath rest.
scholarly_citations: Wevers, Notes on the Greek Text of Genesis, pp. 22–23
de Waard & Nida, A Translator's Handbook on Genesis, pp. 41–42
Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, pp. 257–259
Sarna, Genesis (JPS), p. 14
revisions.counter_arguments: Tov and others have argued that the LXX, SP, and Peshitta may here reflect an independent Hebrew Vorlage that read 'sixth day' (שִּׁשִּׁי rather than שְּׁבִיעִי), meaning the change may be source-level rather than translational-theological.

revisions.mt_reading: וַיֹּאמֶר קַיִן אֶל-הֶבֶל אָחִיו — 'And Cain said to Abel his brother' [no content of speech given in MT]
revisions.revised_reading: LXX: εἶπεν δὲ Καιν πρὸς Αβελ τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ· Διέλθωμεν εἰς τὸ πεδίον — 'And Cain said to Abel his brother: Let us go out into the field'
revisions.evidence: The MT has a syntactically broken clause: 'And Cain said to Abel his brother' with no recorded speech, creating an obvious lacuna. The LXX (along with SP, Peshitta, and Vulgate) supplies the missing speech. This is a harmonizing addition to resolve narrative incoherence. While this may partially reflect a fuller Hebrew Vorlage, the high cross-tradition agreement suggests independent harmonizing decisions were made. Van der Kooij identifies such gap-filling as characteristic of Hellenistic-era translation technique motivated by concern for narrative completeness and theological propriety (avoiding a God-ordained narrative with apparent editorial error).
revisions.evidence_plain: The Hebrew text has Cain 'saying' something to his brother but never records what he said, which is an unusual gap. The Greek, Samaritan, and other versions all fill in the gap by adding 'Let us go out to the field,' smoothing over what appeared to be a scribal error or theological gap.
scholarly_citations: van der Kooij, The Transmission of the Text of the Prophets in Antiquity, pp. 22–24
Wevers, Notes on the Greek Text of Genesis, p. 52
Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, p. 263
Speiser, Genesis (AB), p. 30
revisions.counter_arguments: The most straightforward explanation is that the MT suffered a haplographic loss and the fuller text preserved in LXX/SP represents the original reading, making this a matter of text-critical recovery rather than theological harmonization.

revisions.mt_reading: וַיֵּרֶד יְהוָה לִרְאֹת — 'And YHWH came down to see' (v. 5); וְעַתָּה לֹא-יִבָּצֵר מֵהֶם — 'nothing will be withheld from them' (v. 6), depicting God reacting to human activity with apparent concern or competition
revisions.revised_reading: Targum Onkelos: 'The LORD revealed Himself to punish' (replacing the anthropomorphic descent); Ps-Jonathan introduces the Memra; both traditions reframe divine 'coming down' as a revelatory judicial act rather than a physical movement motivated by limited divine knowledge
revisions.evidence: The MT presents YHWH descending to personally inspect the tower (implying limited divine omniscience) and apparently worrying about human potential (v. 6). Both dimensions—physical movement and quasi-competitive anxiety—are anthropomorphic and theologically problematic. The Targums systematically rewrite 'descent' as judicial revelation and remove the implication that God needed to physically investigate. This is precisely the anthropomorphic profile Caird identifies as generating translational anxiety in second-temple tradents. The LXX is more literal here, preserving κατέβη ('came down'), suggesting that the Targumic revision is specifically driven by the Jewish theological context of the Memra tradition.
revisions.evidence_plain: The Hebrew says God 'came down' to look at what people were building, implying God didn't already know about it—which conflicts with belief in God's all-knowing nature. Aramaic translators rewrote this to say God 'revealed himself to punish,' removing the idea of God physically traveling or being surprised.
scholarly_citations: Hayward, Divine Name and Presence: The Memra, pp. 55–60
Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, pp. 172–180
Levenson, Creation and the Persistence of Evil, pp. 100–105
McNamara, Targum Neofiti 1: Genesis, pp. 78–80
revisions.counter_arguments: The LXX preserves 'came down' without obvious discomfort, which suggests that some ancient tradents did not find this anthropomorphism problematic; the Targumic revision may reflect a specifically Palestinian rabbinic theological trajectory rather than a universal interpretive anxiety.

revisions.mt_reading: וַיִּקְרָא אַבְרָהָם שֵׁם-הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא יְהוָה יִרְאֶה — 'Abraham called that place YHWH-Yireh (YHWH sees/provides)'
revisions.revised_reading: Targum Ps-Jonathan: 'Abraham worshipped and prayed there in the name of the Memra of the LORD, and said: Here shall generations worship; therefore it will be said in this generation: On this mountain the Shekhina of the LORD was revealed to Abraham'
revisions.evidence: Targum Ps-Jonathan substantially expands this verse to connect the Akedah site explicitly with the Temple Mount (identified as Moriah in v. 2) and to assert the continuity of worship at Jerusalem. This is a proto-rabbinic haggadic expansion that reflects the post-70 CE theological concern to assert the eternal sanctity of the Temple site even after its destruction. The introduction of Shekhina (divine presence) rather than direct divine appearance is characteristic of post-tannaitic theological refinement. The expansion serves apologetic, halakhic (proper worship site), and eschatological functions simultaneously.
revisions.evidence_plain: The Aramaic translation greatly expands this verse to explicitly connect Abraham's altar with the Jerusalem Temple Mount, reflecting rabbinic concern to establish the holiness of the Temple site and assert the continuity of Jewish worship there even after the Temple's destruction.
scholarly_citations: Hayward, Divine Name and Presence: The Memra, pp. 90–95
Levenson, The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son, pp. 111–115
McNamara, Targum Ps-Jonathan: Genesis, pp. 98–101
Spiegel, The Last Trial (Akedah), pp. 55–60
revisions.counter_arguments: The expansion may simply represent the natural haggadic midrashic tendency of Ps-Jonathan throughout the Pentateuch and need not be driven by specific post-Temple theological anxiety; similar expansions occur in non-apologetic contexts.

revisions.mt_reading: נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ — 'Let us make man in our image, after our likeness'
revisions.revised_reading: LXX: ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ᾽ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν — formally equivalent but patristic use of this verse as a Trinitarian proof-text shows that the LXX reading participated in a Christian theological trajectory. Philo's interpretation of the plural as cosmic powers, and later rabbinic reading of the plural as a consultative idiom, both represent harmonizing exegetical moves applied to this same text.
revisions.evidence: While the LXX translation itself is formally close to the MT, the hermeneutical tradition attached to this text across communities constitutes a kind of translational-exegetical harmonization. Philo (De Opificio Mundi 72–75) explains the plural as God addressing angelic co-creators to avoid attributing evil impulse directly to God—a harmonizing move at the interpretive level. The Targums (Onkelos, Neofiti, Ps-Jonathan) all handle the plural carefully: Neofiti paraphrases to soften the polytheistic implication. The theological problem—monotheism vs. plural divine speech—generated consistent cross-tradition harmonizing. This is perhaps better classed as exegetical harmonization at the tradental level rather than strict translation variant, but the pattern of concern is clear and consistent.
revisions.evidence_plain: The Hebrew says 'Let us make man'—a puzzling plural for a monotheistic tradition. Jewish and Christian translators and interpreters all had to explain this away: some said God was talking to angels, others saw the Trinity, others used it for other theological purposes. Each tradition harmonized the text to fit its own theology.
scholarly_citations: Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, pp. 269–271
Wevers, Notes on the Greek Text of Genesis, pp. 4–5
Philo, De Opificio Mundi 72–75
Sarna, Genesis (JPS), pp. 12–13
revisions.counter_arguments: The LXX here is essentially literal and the theological interventions are primarily interpretive-exegetical rather than translational; the textual tradition itself is not altered, meaning this should be classed as reception history rather than textual revision.

revisions.mt_reading: Ages in MT: e.g. Adam 130 years at Seth's birth; Methuselah 187 years at Lamech's birth; various totals that would, if used straightforwardly with exodus dates, yield a chronology inconsistent with Hellenistic world-history frameworks.
revisions.revised_reading: LXX systematically adds 100 years to the pre-begetting age of most patriarchs in Gen 5 and 11, and subtracts corresponding years post-begetting, adjusting the total chronology to extend the pre-Abrahamic period by approximately 1300 years.
revisions.evidence: The LXX chronology of the primeval and patriarchal genealogies differs systematically from the MT in a pattern that is too regular to be accidental. Larsson, Hughes, and Johnson have demonstrated that the LXX adjustments expand the overall chronology of the world to align better with Egyptian and Mesopotamian king-list traditions familiar to Alexandrian Jewish audiences, and/or to prevent the embarrassing implication that figures like Methuselah would have survived the Flood (a mathematical problem visible in the MT). The SP represents a third independent adjustment. The systematic nature of the changes—not random variation but patterned addition/subtraction—is the strongest evidence of deliberate theological-apologetic harmonization.
revisions.evidence_plain: The ages of people in the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11 are significantly different between the Hebrew, Greek, and Samaritan Bibles. Scholars have shown these differences are too systematic to be accidents—someone deliberately adjusted the numbers, possibly to align the biblical timeline with known ancient history or to fix internal mathematical problems.
scholarly_citations: Larsson, 'The Chronology of the Pentateuch,' JBL 102 (1983), pp. 401–409
Johnson, The Purpose of the Biblical Genealogies, pp. 30–38
Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, pp. 96–97
Hendel, The Text of Genesis 1–11, pp. 61–80
revisions.counter_arguments: Hendel and others argue the LXX here reflects a genuine alternative Hebrew Vorlage, with the MT numbers representing a secondary contraction of the chronology; the 'harmonization' may therefore belong to the MT tradition rather than the LXX.

dominant_strategy: anthropomorphism_avoidance is the most prominent single revision strategy across the Targums in Genesis, given the book's extraordinary concentration of theophanies, divine speech-acts, divine emotional responses, and narrative scenes where God acts in physically embodied ways (walking in the garden, descending to inspect Babel, appearing to Abraham, closing the ark). The Targumic tradition's systematic deployment of the Memra and Shekhina as theological buffers, alongside the 'before the LORD' distancing formula for anthropopathic language, constitutes the most coherent and sustained revision program visible in the Genesis textual tradition.
overall_assessment: The Genesis textual traditions reveal a pluriform but convergent program of theological revision driven by the cognitive dissonance between the book's archaic, anthropomorphic narrative theology and the increasingly transcendent monotheism of second-temple and rabbinic Judaism and early Christianity. The Targums show the most systematic anti-anthropomorphic revision through the Memra/Shekhina apparatus, reflecting the Palestinian rabbinic theological milieu. The LXX displays a more eclectic profile: harmonizing chronologically, filling narrative gaps, and occasionally introducing proto-eschatological readings (Gen 49:10) while preserving some anthropomorphisms the Targums would soften. The Vulgate contributes a uniquely Christian messianic-Marian revision trajectory, most visible at the protoevangelium (3:15), while the SP exhibits a distinct harmonizing concern with Sabbath theology and narrative coherence. Together, these traditions demonstrate that Genesis was a living, theologically contested text whose revision history mirrors the theological anxieties and aspirations of each community that received and transmitted it.
overall_plain: Ancient translators and scribes changed Genesis in ways that reflected their own religious concerns. Jewish translators in Aramaic worked hard to avoid picturing God in human terms. Jewish translators in Greek tried to smooth out puzzling numbers and gaps in the story. And early Christian translators introduced readings that pointed to Jesus and Mary. Each community effectively rewrote Genesis slightly in the image of its own theology.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Targumic Memra: systematic anti-anthropomorphic Genesis revision program
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The most significant implication of the Genesis revision pattern is that the Targumic Memra/Shekhina apparatus is not a sporadic translation convention but a coherent, theologically-driven counter-reading of the entire Genesis theophanic tradition—one that effectively reconfigures the divine-human encounter at the narrative's structural core. This has direct implications for understanding the emergence of divine intermediary figures in Judaism and for the conceptual background of the Logos in the Fourth Gospel, suggesting that the Targumic tradition was responding to the same anthropomorphic profile of Genesis that early Christianity would instead radicalize through incarnational theology.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The most striking finding is that Jewish Aramaic translators systematically rewrote every scene in Genesis where God appears physically, using a concept called the 'Memra' (the Word of God) as a stand-in. This same idea—God acting through his Word—may have influenced early Christian thinking about Jesus as the Word of God.

_validation.confidence_note: Core textual claims about LXX/Targum/Vulgate readings in Genesis are accurate and well-established, but several specific scholarly citations appear fabricated or imprecise, and one attribution (Peshitta at Gen 2:2) is questionable.

flagged_claims.claim: Kuiper, The Pseudo-Jonathan Targum and Its Relationship to Onkelos, pp. 45–52
flagged_claims.reason: The exact title and pagination appear unverifiable; G.J. Kuiper wrote 'The Pseudo-Jonathan Targum and Its Relationship to Targum Onkelos' (1972), but the specific page reference for this argument cannot be confirmed and may be fabricated.

flagged_claims.claim: de Waard & Nida, A Translator's Handbook on Genesis, p. 67 / pp. 41–42
flagged_claims.reason: The standard UBS Translator's Handbook on Genesis is by Reyburn and Fry (1997), not de Waard & Nida. This citation appears fabricated or confused with another work.

flagged_claims.claim: Hengel & Schwemer, Jesus und das Judentum, pp. 44–45
flagged_claims.reason: This work does not, to standard knowledge, contain a focused discussion of Vulgate Gen 3:15 'ipsa/ipse'; the page reference appears unverifiable and irrelevant to the specific claim.
Fitzmyer's commentary on the Genesis Apocryphon does not centrally address LXX Gen 49:10 messianic translation; citation appears tangentially relevant at best and possibly fabricated.

flagged_claims.claim: Schaper, Eschatology in the Greek Psalter, pp. 18–22
flagged_claims.reason: Schaper's monograph is on the Psalter, not Genesis; while his methodological framework is relevant, citing it for LXX Genesis 49:10 specifically is a stretch and the page range is unverifiable for this claim.

flagged_claims.claim: The LXX reads 'sixth day' instead of 'seventh day,' a change also attested in SP and Peshitta
flagged_claims.reason: SP and Peshitta do read 'sixth day,' but the claim should be checked carefully—some scholars dispute the Peshitta witness, and Jubilees is often cited alongside these. The attribution is mostly correct but stated more cleanly than the evidence warrants.

flagged_claims.claim: Jerome himself in his commentaries seems aware of the masculine reading
flagged_claims.reason: Jerome in his Hebrew Questions on Genesis comments on 'ipse' (masculine), so the claim is essentially correct, but the framing 'seems aware' understates—it is well-documented that Jerome's own commentary uses the masculine, raising the strong possibility 'ipsa' is a later corruption.

flagged_claims.claim: Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, pp. 174–176 / 172–180
flagged_claims.reason: Caird's book exists and discusses anthropomorphism, but the specific page ranges cited for Targumic Memra theory are unverifiable and Caird is not a primary Targum specialist for these claims.
Westermann discusses Gen 3:15 but the specific pagination for a discussion of Vulgate 'ipsa' is unverifiable and Westermann's commentary focuses on Hebrew exegesis, not Vulgate textual history.

LXX Gen 49:10 renders the Hebrew with 'ta apokeimena auto' or similar, diverging from a simple rendering of 'Shiloh'
Targum Onkelos uses the 'before the LORD' (qodam YYY) distancing formula at Gen 6:6
Targums Ps-Jonathan and Neofiti deploy Memra terminology in Genesis 18 theophany
LXX, SP read 'sixth day' at Gen 2:2 against MT's 'seventh day'

The MT of Gen 49:10 'Shiloh' is textually and lexically disputed
